fact: Angels Flight first climbed Bunker Hill on December 31, 1901. A ride cost 1 cent, or 3 rides for a nickel, and over 2,000 people rode it on opening day.
source_title: Angels Flight: Welcome Back, Olivet and Sinai
source_author: Kelly Wallace

fact: Koreatown's story traces to 1902, when independence activist Dosan Ahn Chang Ho immigrated to the U.S. with his wife Helen Ahn.
source_title: The History of Koreatown: A Heartbeat of Los Angeles
source_author: Joann Im

fact: City parks superintendent Joseph Henry Tomlinson chose the name because of echoes he heard during the construction of Echo Park Lake in 1892.
source_title: Where did the name Echo Park come from? Should we hear echoes?
source_author: Chris Nichols

fact: Boyle Heights has been called the "Ellis Island" of the West Coast, home to many immigrant groups shut out of other LA neighborhoods.
source_title: Boyle Heights Oral History
source_author: Anita Martinez, Digitization & Special Collections

fact: Since Griffith Observatory opened in 1935, more than seven million people have looked through its 12-inch Zeiss telescope, more than any other telescope in the world.
source_title: Zeiss Telescopes

fact: San Pedro was established as its own city in 1888 and grew once the Southern Pacific Railroad linked LA to the transcontinental network.
source_title: Comments on San Pedro Community Plan Update Draft EIR

fact: In 1906 LA annexed the "Shoestring," a strip under a mile wide and 16 miles long, so it could reach the harbor. San Pedro and Wilmington joined months later.
source_title: The Shoestring Strip: Los Angeles Goes Out on a Limb
source_note: Original source: Homer Hamlin, City Engineer, "Map showing territory annexed to the city of Los Angeles" (1916), Library of Congress: http://www.loc.gov/resource/g4364l.ct001800/

fact: Simon Rodia bought a triangular lot in Watts in 1921 and spent more than three decades building 17 structures by hand, with towers reaching nearly 100 feet.
source_title: Watts Towers Recognized by World Monuments Fund
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Cultural Affairs

fact: The Los Angeles chapter of the NAACP was founded in the sitting room of dentists John and Vada Somerville, USC's first Black graduates.
source_title: Dunbar Hotel: The Jewel of Central Avenue
source_author: Mary McCoy, Senior Librarian

fact: The Dunbar Hotel on Central Avenue opened June 23, 1928 as the Hotel Somerville, the first hotel built by and for Black people. It hosted the first NAACP convention held in Los Angeles days later.
source_title: Dunbar Hotel: The Jewel of Central Avenue
source_author: Mary McCoy, Senior Librarian

fact: The house used as the McFly family residence in the 1985 film Back to the Future is located at 9303 Roslyndale Avenue in Arleta and was built in 1954.
source_title: LRS UNSEATED: The Valley

fact: The Arleta Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners on October 22, 2002, under Certification Order 53.
source_title: Arleta Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: The 10-mile Pacoima Wash stormwater corridor runs from the base of the San Gabriel Mountains in Sylmar down to its confluence with the Tujunga Wash in Arleta.
source_title: Pacoima Beautiful: Reorienting a Neighborhood That No Longer Suits Our Needs

fact: Beachy Avenue Elementary School was already an active neighborhood hub in Arleta prior to the community's formal 1968 separation from Pacoima, hosting annual community talent shows documented in the Valley Times.
source_title: In you go
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph: Valley Times Collection, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: In the 1960s, residents in the western half of Pacoima led a petition to break away and form an independent neighborhood named Arleta, which was officially recognized in 1968.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Founded in 1912 as Owensmouth—marking the western terminus of the Los Angeles Aqueduct distribution system—the community voted to rename itself Canoga Park in 1931.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: The Los Angeles River officially begins in Canoga Park at the confluence of Bell Creek and Arroyo Calabasas behind Canoga Park High School.
source_title: Los Angeles River Master Plan

fact: During the 1950s and 1960s, Rocketdyne established major rocket engine research and manufacturing facilities in Canoga Park that built propulsion systems for the Apollo moon landings and the Space Shuttle.
source_title: Rocketdyne and the San Fernando Valley's Aerospace Boom

fact: Built in 1924 in Mission Revival style at 7260 Owensmouth Avenue, the Canoga Park Branch Library (formerly the Owensmouth Branch Library) is designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 312.
source_title: Canoga Park Branch Library

fact: The Canoga Park Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2003 to represent the historic downtown Sherman Way corridor and surrounding neighborhoods.
source_title: Canoga Park Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Between 1900 and 1904, Southern Pacific Railroad crews bored three tunnels totaling over 7,300 feet through the Santa Susana Mountains at Chatsworth, completing the Coast Line link between Los Angeles and San Francisco.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Originally named Chatsworth Park after Chatsworth House in Derbyshire, England, the community was founded in 1888 by developer George R. Crow along the Southern Pacific Railroad line.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Santa Susana Pass State Historic Park in Chatsworth preserves remnants of the Old Santa Susana Stage Road, which served as the primary stagecoach and mail route between Los Angeles and Ventura from 1861 until 1876.
source_title: Santa Susana Pass State Historic Park

fact: Built in 1893 out of locally quarried sandstone at 10385 Shadow Oak Drive, the Minnie Hill Palmer House (Homestead Acre) is the oldest surviving wooden-and-stone residence in Chatsworth and is designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 133.
source_title: Chatsworth History & Homestead Acre

fact: During the silent and studio eras, the Iverson Movie Ranch in Chatsworth served as the filming location for more than 2,000 motion pictures and television episodes, including Stagecoach and The Lone Ranger.
source_title: Chatsworth's Iverson Movie Ranch: Hollywood's Favorite Western Backdrop

fact: Encino takes its name from Rancho Los Encinos ('Ranch of the Live Oaks'), a 4,460-acre Mexican land grant awarded in 1845 to three Mission San Fernando Gabrielino-Tongva leaders: Ramón, Francisco, and Roque.
source_title: Los Encinos State Historic Park

fact: The Encino Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent residential and Ventura Boulevard corridor stakeholders.
source_title: Encino Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Standing at the intersection of Louise and Ventura Boulevards in Encino, the Encino Oak Tree was estimated to be over 1,000 years old and designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 24 before falling in a 1998 storm.
source_title: The Encino Oak: Remembering a 1,000-Year-Old Valley Landmark

fact: Built in 1849 by Vincente de la Osa at 16756 Moorpark Street, the nine-room De la Osa Adobe in Encino served as a prominent stagecoach stop along El Camino Real and is California Historical Landmark No. 689.
source_title: Los Encinos State Historic Park

fact: On August 5, 1769, the Spanish Portolá expedition camped beside the natural springs at Los Encinos, marking the first recorded European entry into the San Fernando Valley.
source_title: Los Encinos State Historic Park

fact: In the 1940s, western film actor John Carpenter relocated his Heaven on Earth Ranch to Lake View Terrace, where visitors rode horses and toured a mock western town.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Following the devastating March 1938 flood, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built Hansen Dam across Tujunga Wash in Lake View Terrace, completing the 10,475-foot-long earthen flood-control structure in 1940.
source_title: Five Most Fascinating L.A. Dams, Where Disasters Struck and Catastrophes Were Averted

fact: The Foothill Trails District Neighborhood Council was certified on March 25, 2003, under Certification Order 66, representing Lake View Terrace, La Tuna Canyon, and Shadow Hills.
source_title: Foothill Trails District Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: During the Great Depression, La Tuna Canyon in the Foothill Trails District housed California Conservation Corps camps that constructed flood-control infrastructure in the Verdugo Mountains.
source_title: The Valley Paradox: Gentlemen Farming and Immigrant Labor in the Creation of San Fernando Valley

fact: The Lake View Terrace Branch Library at 12002 Osborne Street was designed as an eco-friendly civic building featuring bamboo flooring, drought-tolerant native landscaping, and an exterior horse-hitching post.
source_title: Lake View Terrace Branch Library - A Guide to Eco-Friendly Design

fact: In 1927, the Sunshine Ranch in northern Granada Hills planted thousands of citrus and walnut trees irrigated by newly available Los Angeles Aqueduct water from the nearby Van Norman reservoirs.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Founded in 1926 as the agricultural subdivision of Granada, the community added 'Hills' to its name in 1942 to reflect its foothill topography below the Santa Susana Mountains.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: O'Melveny Park in Granada Hills North spans 672 acres in Bee Canyon, making it the second-largest public park in the City of Los Angeles after Griffith Park.
source_title: O'Melveny Park
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: Completed in 1915 in Granada Hills North, the Lower San Fernando Dam was heavily damaged during the February 9, 1971 Sylmar Earthquake, forcing the evacuation of 80,000 Valley residents downstream.
source_title: February 1971 - 6.6 Sylmar Earthquake Shakes the Southland
source_author: Elson Trinidad

fact: The Granada Hills North Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent the northern foothill and residential areas north of Rinaldi Street.
source_title: Granada Hills North Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: The White Oak Avenue corridor in Granada Hills South is lined with mature deodar cedar trees planted in 1932 by the San Fernando Valley Garden Club as a civic beautification project.
source_title: Granada Hills Deodar Cedar Trees

fact: Developed between 1949 and 1951 in Granada Hills South, the Balboa Highlands neighborhood is a collection of over 100 Mid-Century Modern homes built by Joseph Eichler and designed by architects Jones & Emmons and Claude Oakland.
source_title: Balboa Highlands Historic Preservation Overlay Zone (HPOZ)

fact: The Balboa Highlands tract in Granada Hills South represents the only Eichler-built subdivision ever constructed in the City of Los Angeles.
source_title: Balboa Highlands

fact: Originally opened in 1929 as the Granada Hills deposit station, the Granada Hills Branch Library moved into its dedicated civic facility on Chatsworth Street in Granada Hills South in 1957.
source_title: History of the Granada Hills Branch Library

fact: The Granada Hills South Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2005 after residents petitioned to establish a dedicated council for the commercial and residential core south of Rinaldi Street.
source_title: Granada Hills South Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: The Greater Toluca Lake Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent Toluca Lake, Toluca Woods, and West Toluca Lake.
source_title: Greater Toluca Lake Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: During the early twentieth century, the Toluca Lake and North Hollywood area contained a major concentration of municipal water wells linked to the Silver Lake Reservoir via the River Conduit.
source_title: Los Angeles Citywide Historic Context Statement: Municipal Water and Power, 1902-1980

fact: Toluca Lake was established in 1923 when developers subdivided former ranchland into a lakeside residential enclave resurrecting the historic 'Toluca' name once used by neighboring North Hollywood.
source_title: When North Hollywood Was a Town Named Toluca, or Lankershim

fact: The Toluca Lake Chamber of Commerce was formed in 1939 to represent local businesses along the Riverside Drive commercial corridor.
source_title: Fall 2022 - Commemorating the Centennial of Toluca Lake
source_author: Fritz Coleman

fact: Entertainer Bob Hope and his wife Dolores lived for decades at their historic estate in Toluca Lake, later hosted by the Los Angeles Conservancy for preservation events.
source_title: Fall 2022 - L.A. Conservancy Benefit Honors Local History

fact: The Greater Valley Glen Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent neighborhoods bounded by Sherman Way, the 170 Freeway, Burbank Boulevard, and Hazeltine Avenue.
source_title: Greater Valley Glen Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Painted along the Tujunga Wash flood control wall in Valley Glen starting in 1976 under artist Judith Baca, The Great Wall of Los Angeles is a half-mile-long mural depicting California's multicultural history.
source_title: The Great Wall of Los Angeles
source_publisher: Social and Public Art Resource Center (SPARC)

fact: Founded in 1949 in Greater Valley Glen, Los Angeles Valley College occupies a 105-acre campus serving the central San Fernando Valley.
source_title: Neighborhood History: A Look Into the Past

fact: Spanning 4.8 square miles in the central San Fernando Valley, Greater Valley Glen is bisected north-to-south by the Tujunga Wash flood-control channel.
source_title: Neighborhood History: A Look Into the Past

fact: Originally divided between Van Nuys and North Hollywood, Valley Glen was officially recognized as a distinct neighborhood by the City of Los Angeles in 1998 following a resident beautification and identity campaign.
source_title: Neighborhood History: A Look Into the Past

fact: Originally part of western Van Nuys, the neighborhood was formally recognized by the Los Angeles City Council as the distinct community of Lake Balboa in 2006.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Opened in 1992 within the Sepulveda Basin, the 27-acre Lake Balboa is filled with reclaimed water from the adjacent Donald C. Tillman Water Reclamation Plant and is lined with over 2,000 pink cloud cherry blossom trees.
source_title: Lake Balboa / Anthony C. Beilenson Park
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: Designed by Dr. Koichi Kawana and opened in 1984 in Lake Balboa, SuihoEn ('The Japanese Garden') spans 6.5 acres on the grounds of the Tillman Water Reclamation Plant.
source_title: The Japanese Garden (SuihoEn) History

fact: The Lake Balboa Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2004, representing communities north of the Sepulveda Basin between the I-405 and White Oak Avenue.
source_title: Lake Balboa Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Completed in 1941 by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers across the Los Angeles River, Sepulveda Dam in Lake Balboa creates a 2,000-acre flood-control basin and regional recreation area.
source_title: Sepulveda Basin Recreation Area
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: San Fernando Mission Boulevard in Mission Hills was originally named Stanford Avenue after former California Governor Leland Stanford, who loaned Charles Maclay the funds to purchase northern Valley land in 1874.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: In the late nineteenth century, Lopez Station on the 15700 block of Rinaldi Street in Mission Hills served as a Butterfield Stage stop along the route between Los Angeles and San Francisco.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Brand Park—also known as Memory Garden—across from Mission San Fernando was deeded to the City of Los Angeles on November 4, 1920, and designated a historic landmark in 1935.
source_title: Brand Park entrance, Mission Hills
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph by Herman Schultheis, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: Located at 10940 Sepulveda Boulevard in Mission Hills, the Andres Pico Adobe is the second-oldest surviving adobe residence in the City of Los Angeles.
source_title: Andres Pico Adobe
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: Founded by Father Fermín Lasuén on September 8, 1797, Mission San Fernando Rey de España in Mission Hills was the seventeenth Spanish mission established in Alta California.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Constructed in 1895 at 11275 Chandler Boulevard in NoHo, the Southern Pacific Lankershim Depot is the San Fernando Valley's oldest unmodified railroad structure.
source_title: Lankershim Depot

fact: Founded in 1888 by James B. Lankershim and Isaac Lankershim on 12,000 acres of former wheat ranchland, the community was known as Toluca and then Lankershim before business owners renamed it North Hollywood in 1927.
source_title: When North Hollywood Was a Town Named Toluca, or Lankershim

fact: Opened in 1926 at 5231 Lankershim Boulevard in NoHo, the Spanish Colonial Revival El Portal Theatre originally hosted vaudeville and silent films and is designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 573.
source_title: El Portal Theatre

fact: The NoHo Neighborhood Council (Mid-Town North Hollywood) was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent the NoHo Arts District and central North Hollywood.
source_title: Mid-Town North Hollywood Neighborhood Council (NoHo)
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Opened in 1930 at 5211 Tujunga Avenue in NoHo, the Amelia Earhart North Hollywood Regional Branch Library was renamed in 1980 in honor of the aviation pioneer who lived in the neighborhood.
source_title: History of the North Hollywood Amelia Earhart Regional Branch Library

fact: The North Hills East Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners on September 14, 2010.
source_title: North Hills East Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: In the early 1990s, the community of Sepulveda was renamed North Hills, and the city divided the area along the I-405 freeway into North Hills East and North Hills West.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: North Hills was originally an agricultural settlement named Mission Acres before residents voted in 1927 to rename the community Sepulveda in honor of early California landowner Francisco Sepulveda.
source_title: First-Time Buyers Like Low Prices, Accessibility : Sepulveda

fact: The post-World War II suburban boom brought landmark commercial corridors to North Hills and neighboring Mission Hills along Sepulveda Boulevard, including the 1950 opening of Miracle Market at Nordhoff and Sepulveda.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: The Sepulveda Unitarian Universalist Society Sanctuary at 9550 Haskell Avenue in North Hills East, designed by architect Frank Ehrenthal in 1964 and nicknamed "The Onion," was designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 975 in 2010.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Following the January 17, 1994 Northridge Earthquake, several buildings at the Sepulveda VA campus in North Hills West sustained structural damage, leading to seismic retrofitting and modernization of its outpatient facilities.
source_title: 1994 Northridge Earthquake

fact: During the 1920s and 1930s, North Hills West was dominated by small poultry ranches and walnut orchards subdivided under the Mission Acres Land Company.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: The North Hills West Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2004 to represent neighborhoods west of the San Diego Freeway (I-405) between Devonshire and Roscoe.
source_title: North Hills West Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Originally settled in the 1910s as the farming community of Mission Acres, the area was renamed Sepulveda in 1927 before residents voted in the early 1990s to adopt the name North Hills.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Located at 16111 Plummer Street in North Hills West, the Sepulveda Ambulatory Care Center (formerly the Sepulveda VA Medical Center) opened in 1955 on a 160-acre campus to serve World War II and Korean War veterans.
source_title: VA Sepulveda Ambulatory Care Center History

fact: In 1923, the City of Los Angeles annexed the Lankershim territory—including modern North Hollywood Northeast—incorporating its rapidly growing orchards and subdivisions into the city.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: During the 1890s and 1900s, the agricultural lands of northern Lankershim (now North Hollywood Northeast) were famous across Southern California for large-scale peach, apricot, plum, and pear orchards.
source_title: When North Hollywood Was a Town Named Toluca, or Lankershim

fact: Following World War II, major aviation and defense manufacturing expanded along the Hollywood Burbank Airport corridor bordering North Hollywood Northeast, driving rapid suburban tract housing.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Lankershim Boulevard, which runs north-south through North Hollywood Northeast, was named in 1906 after developer James B. Lankershim when the local post office officially adopted the Lankershim name.
source_title: When North Hollywood Was a Town Named Toluca, or Lankershim

fact: The North Hollywood Northeast Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2003 to represent communities north of Victory Boulevard and east of the 170 Freeway.
source_title: North Hollywood Northeast Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: The North Hollywood West Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2003 to represent neighborhoods bounded by Sherman Way, the 170 Freeway, Burbank Boulevard, and Coldwater Canyon.
source_title: North Hollywood West Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: James Madison Middle School on Hart Street in North Hollywood West opened in 1955 to serve the surge of postwar families moving into single-family tracts between Coldwater Canyon and the 170 Freeway.
source_title: North Hollywood-Valley Village Community Plan

fact: Whitsett Fields Park and the adjacent LADWP spreading grounds in North Hollywood West capture storm runoff from the Tujunga Wash to recharge the San Fernando Groundwater Basin.
source_title: Tujunga Spreading Grounds Enhancement Project
source_publisher: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP)

fact: North Hollywood West was originally part of the 47,000-acre Lankershim-Van Nuys ranch syndicate tract opened to farming and suburban subdivision following the 1913 arrival of the Los Angeles Aqueduct.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Completed through North Hollywood in the 1960s, the Hollywood Freeway (State Route 170) forms the eastern boundary of North Hollywood West, separating it from central North Hollywood.
source_title: North Hollywood-Valley Village Community Plan

fact: Founded in 1910 as Zelzah—a biblical oasis name—the community changed its name to North Los Angeles in 1929 before adopting the name Northridge in 1938.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Opened in 1973 at the center of the CSUN campus in Northridge East, the Delmar T. Oviatt Library was featured as Starfleet Academy in the 2009 film Star Trek.
source_title: CSUN University Library History

fact: California State University, Northridge (CSUN) in Northridge East began in 1956 as the San Fernando Valley Campus of Los Angeles State College before becoming an independent institution in 1958.
source_title: CSUN History

fact: The Northridge East Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2003, encompassing the CSUN campus and surrounding residential neighborhoods east of Reseda Boulevard.
source_title: Northridge East Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: During the 1930s and 1940s, Northridge East was known as the 'Horse Capital of the West,' home to thoroughbred breeding farms owned by celebrities including Barbara Stanwyck and Zeppo Marx.
source_title: Northridge's Equestrian Past: When Thoroughbreds Ruled the Valley

fact: Originally established in 1914 in the Zelzah schoolhouse, the Northridge Branch Library relocated to its current facility at 9051 Darby Avenue in Northridge South in 1966.
source_title: History of the Northridge Branch Library

fact: Northridge Hospital Medical Center on Roscoe Boulevard in Northridge South has served as one of the San Fernando Valley's primary trauma centers since opening in 1955.
source_title: Northridge Hospital Medical Center History

fact: The Northridge Meadows apartment complex at 9565 Reseda Boulevard in Northridge South suffered a catastrophic soft-story collapse during the 1994 earthquake, prompting Los Angeles to enact mandatory seismic retrofit ordinances.
source_title: Remembering the 1994 Northridge Earthquake

fact: On January 17, 1994 at 4:30 a.m., the magnitude 6.7 Northridge Earthquake struck on a blind thrust fault beneath Northridge South and neighboring Reseda, causing over $20 billion in damage across Southern California.
source_title: 1994 Northridge Earthquake

fact: The Northridge South Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2010 after local residents formed a dedicated council for the commercial and residential area south of Nordhoff Street.
source_title: Northridge South Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: In 1929, the Southern Pacific Railroad renamed its Zelzah station in Northridge to North Los Angeles after local ranchers successfully lobbied for a stronger geographic identity.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Nobel Charter Middle School and surrounding neighborhoods in Northridge West were developed in the 1950s and 1960s on former citrus groves irrigated by the San Fernando Valley's early water distribution network.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: The Northridge West Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2005 to represent communities west of Reseda Boulevard between Devonshire and Nordhoff.
source_title: Northridge West Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: During the 1994 Northridge Earthquake, two multi-level concrete parking structures at Northridge Fashion Center in Northridge West collapsed, leading to nationwide revisions in precast concrete building codes.
source_title: 1994 Northridge Earthquake

fact: Northridge Fashion Center, located on Tampa Avenue in Northridge West, opened in 1971 as the San Fernando Valley's largest enclosed regional shopping mall.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: By the 1930s, restrictive racial covenants across the San Fernando Valley concentrated Mexican and Black agricultural workers in Pacoima and neighboring San Fernando.
source_title: The Valley Paradox: Gentlemen Farming and Immigrant Labor in the Creation of San Fernando Valley

fact: Pacoima takes its name from the indigenous Tataviam settlement of "Pacoinga Village," a Tataviam word translating to "the entrance" (la entrada).
source_title: Historical Timeline of Pacoima

fact: In 1912, developers briefly renamed Pacoima "Mulholland" for one year in an attempt to boost real estate sales using Los Angeles Aqueduct chief engineer William Mulholland's fame.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: In 1951, developers built the Joe Louis Homes housing tract in Pacoima—named after the heavyweight boxing champion—helping establish one of Southern California's earliest postwar Black middle-class suburbs.
source_title: Historical Timeline of Pacoima

fact: Following their release from World War II internment camps, returning Japanese American residents founded the San Fernando Valley Japanese American Community Center in Pacoima.
source_title: Historical Timeline of Pacoima

fact: Panorama City was developed in the late 1940s on the former Panorama Ranch by Fritz Burns and industrialist Henry J. Kaiser as the first master-planned postwar community in the San Fernando Valley.
source_title: Panorama City

fact: Promotional campaigns for Panorama City marketed the planned neighborhood as featuring "22 miles of homes" anchored by a dedicated regional shopping district at Van Nuys and Roscoe Boulevards.
source_title: How We Got This Way (Los Angeles has Always Been Suburban)

fact: Designed by architects Wurdeman & Becket, the Panorama City master plan called for more than 4,000 Ranch and Minimal Traditional homes priced under $10,000 for returning World War II veterans.
source_title: Panorama City

fact: By 1951, Panorama City's rapid postwar buildout had reached 7,000 completed homes and a new population of roughly 20,000 residents.
source_title: Panorama City shows astounding growth
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph: Valley Times Collection, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: In 1947, General Motors opened a major Chevrolet assembly plant in Panorama City that produced the Corvair, Nova, Camaro, and Pontiac Firebird until its closure in 1992.
source_title: Plenty of parking
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph: Valley Times Collection, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: The Porter Ranch Branch Library at 11371 Tampa Avenue opened in 2002 as part of the Los Angeles Public Library's voter-approved 1998 Branch Facilities Bond Program.
source_title: History of the Porter Ranch Branch Library

fact: Porter Ranch is named after Benjamin F. Porter, who in 1874 partnered with George K. Porter and Charles Maclay to purchase 56,000 acres of the northern San Fernando Valley for $115,000.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: The neighborhood was annexed into the City of Los Angeles in 1965, enabling the master-planned suburban development of Porter Ranch along the Santa Susana foothills.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Between October 23, 2015 and February 11, 2016, a blowout at the Aliso Canyon underground natural gas storage facility above Porter Ranch released nearly 100,000 metric tons of methane, forcing the temporary relocation of over 8,000 households.
source_title: Aliso Canyon Natural Gas Leak

fact: The Porter Ranch Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2003 to represent the northernmost foothill neighborhoods west of the I-5/SR-14 interchange.
source_title: Porter Ranch Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: During the 1980s, the Reseda Country Club at 18415 Sherman Way served as one of Southern California's premier live music venues, hosting performances by U2, Tom Petty, The Ramones, and James Brown.
source_title: When the Reseda Country Club Was the Center of the Valley's Music Scene

fact: Opened in 1948 at 18447 Sherman Way, the Reseda Theater features a Streamline Moderne marquee and tower designed by architect S. Charles Lee and is designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 1138.
source_title: Reseda Theater

fact: Founded in 1912 as Marian—named after Marian Otis Chandler, daughter of Los Angeles Times publisher Harrison Gray Otis—the community adopted the name Reseda after a Southern Pacific Railroad siding named for the fragrant mignonette plant (Reseda odorata).
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: The Reseda Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2003 to represent the central Valley community.
source_title: Reseda Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: In the 1910s, Reseda was developed as a center for poultry and rabbit farming, walnut groves, and sugar beet cultivation irrigated by the Los Angeles Aqueduct.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Opened in 1980 at the corner of Sepulveda and Ventura Boulevards in Sherman Oaks, the Sherman Oaks Galleria popularized 'Valley Girl' youth culture and served as a filming location for Fast Times at Ridgemont High and Commando.
source_title: Sherman Oaks Galleria and the Birth of Valley Girl Culture

fact: Completed in 1957 along the Los Angeles River in Sherman Oaks, the Van Nuys Sherman Oaks War Memorial Park honors San Fernando Valley service members who died in World War II and the Korean War.
source_title: Van Nuys Sherman Oaks Recreation Center
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: Built in 1968 at 15233 Ventura Boulevard in Sherman Oaks, the Mid-Century Modern Union Bank building designed by Albert C. Martin & Associates is a notable commercial landmark along the Ventura corridor.
source_title: Sherman Oaks-Studio City-Toluca Lake-Cahuenga Pass Community Plan

fact: The Sherman Oaks Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent residential hillside and flatland neighborhoods between Mulholland Drive and Burbank Boulevard.
source_title: Sherman Oaks Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Sherman Oaks was founded in 1927 when Los Angeles Pacific Land Company general manager General Moses Hazeltine Sherman subdivided 1,000 acres of company land at $780 per acre.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Designed in 1938 by architect Rudolph Schindler at 4240 Agnes Avenue in Studio City, the modernist Samuel and Dorothy Freeman-style Southall House (Southall Residence) is designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 402.
source_title: Southall Residence

fact: Fryman Canyon Park in Studio City preserves 122 acres of Santa Monica Mountains chaparral and oak woodland along Betty Dearing Trail, connecting to Wilacre Park and Coldwater Canyon Park.
source_title: Fryman Canyon Park

fact: The Studio City Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent Studio City residents and businesses from Mulholland Drive north to Whipple Street.
source_title: Studio City Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Originally known as Laurelwood, Studio City received its name in 1927 when silent film producer Mack Sennett began constructing a 20-acre motion picture studio lot along Ventura Boulevard.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Mack Sennett's 1928 Studio City lot at 4024 Radford Avenue later became Republic Pictures and CBS Studio Center, hosting productions ranging from High Noon to Seinfeld and Mary Tyler Moore.
source_title: CBS Studio Center (Mack Sennett Studios)

fact: For decades, Sun Valley's gravel pits supplied the majority of sand and aggregates used to build Los Angeles, with roughly 1,200 of its 2,600 acres zoned for heavy industry.
source_title: Sun Valley Renaissance

fact: The commercial heart of Sun Valley grew around the intersection of Sunland Boulevard and San Fernando Road, anchored by longtime local fixtures such as Roscoe Hardware.
source_title: Center of Sun Valley
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph dated December 31, 1948, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: Roscoe Boulevard in Sun Valley originated as a single plowed furrow stretching across the San Fernando Valley floor to mark an early property boundary.
source_title: SFV Street Name Origins

fact: In February 1947, the Housing Authority of the City of Los Angeles opened the Basilone Homes veterans housing project at 10160 Glenoaks Boulevard in Roscoe (now Sun Valley), housing more than 140 World War II veterans and their families.
source_title: New homes for veterans
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph: Herald-Examiner Collection, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: Originally named Roscoe after a Southern Pacific Railroad siding, the community adopted the name Sun Valley following a local resident vote.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Sunland was annexed into the City of Los Angeles on August 4, 1926, while neighboring Tujunga remained an independent municipality until joining Los Angeles on March 8, 1932.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Built in 1913 out of river boulders as the clubhouse for William Ellsworth Smythe's utopian "Little Landers" colony, Bolton Hall at 10110 Commerce Avenue later served as Tujunga City Hall, a jail, and a library.
source_title: Bolton Hall: The Little Landers of Tujunga and the Boom and Bust of a Utopian Garden City
source_author: Paul Greenstein

fact: Sunland began in 1885 as the settlement of Monte Vista when 2,200 acres of the Tujunga Park tract were subdivided into 5- to 40-acre agricultural parcels.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: California Poet Laureate and U.S. Representative John S. McGroarty resided in Tujunga, where the local municipal fire station and civic center were built along Foothill Boulevard.
source_title: Noted for McGroarty, dignity
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph: Valley Times Collection, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: The first public library branch in Sunland opened on Fenwick Street in 1914 under Los Angeles County Library supervision before transferring to the Los Angeles Public Library system in 1932.
source_title: History of the Sunland - Tujunga Branch Library

fact: Built between 1916 and 1917 at 13355 San Fernando Road, the Olive Switching Station in Sylmar is the oldest electrical switching facility of the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
source_title: Olive Switching Station
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original documentation: Historic American Buildings Survey (CA-2664).

fact: The Sylmar Packing Corporation at 448 South Hill Street processed harvests from what was once the largest olive grove in the world, employing over 150 workers before its demolition in 1958.
source_title: Sylmar Packing Corporation
source_publisher: Los Angeles Public Library Photo Collection
source_note: Original photograph: Valley Times Collection, Los Angeles Public Library.

fact: Both the original 1913 Los Angeles Aqueduct Cascades and the 1970 Second Los Angeles Aqueduct Cascades terminate in Sylmar, channeling Eastern Sierra water into the Van Norman reservoir complex.
source_title: The Second Los Angeles Aqueduct

fact: The February 9, 1971 magnitude 6.6 Sylmar Earthquake severely damaged Olive View Hospital in Sylmar, prompting California lawmakers to pass the Alquist Hospital Seismic Safety Act in 1973.
source_title: February 1971 - 6.6 Sylmar Earthquake Shakes the Southland
source_author: Elson Trinidad

fact: Established in 1892 as Morningside Cemetery and declared California Historical Landmark No. 753 in 1961, Pioneer Memorial Cemetery in Sylmar is the oldest nonsectarian cemetery in the San Fernando Valley.
source_title: What Lies Beneath: The Many Mysteries of Pioneer Cemetery

fact: Built in 1927 at 18354 Ventura Boulevard in Tarzana, the Edgar Rice Burroughs Inc. headquarters building housed the author's literary archive and publishing operations for nearly a century.
source_title: Edgar Rice Burroughs Building

fact: Located in the Santa Monica Mountains above Tarzana, Marvin Braude Mulholland Gateway Park provides trailhead access to more than 20,000 acres of protected parkland in Topanga State Park and Big Wild.
source_title: Marvin Braude Mulholland Gateway Park

fact: The Tarzana Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2003 to represent residents and businesses from Victory Boulevard south into the Santa Monica Mountains.
source_title: Tarzana Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Tarzana is named after Tarzan of the Apes creator Edgar Rice Burroughs, who in 1919 purchased the 550-acre Mil Flores estate from Los Angeles Times publisher Harrison Gray Otis and renamed it Tarzana Ranch.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: In 1922, Edgar Rice Burroughs subdivided portions of Tarzana Ranch into small agricultural lots, and the U.S. Post Office officially recognized the community name Tarzana on December 12, 1930.
source_title: Edgar Rice Burroughs and the Founding of Tarzana

fact: Valley Village Park, located at 5000 Westpark Drive, provides neighborhood green space alongside the Tujunga Wash greenway corridor.
source_title: Valley Village Park
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: Valley Village originated in the late 1930s as a residential subdivision west of North Hollywood and was formally recognized as an independent Los Angeles neighborhood in 1991 following a community campaign.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Opened in 1939 at 5230 Laurel Canyon Boulevard in Valley Village, North Hollywood High School's historic campus features WPA-era Streamline Moderne architecture.
source_title: North Hollywood-Valley Village Community Plan

fact: During the 1930s and 1940s, Valley Village attracted numerous motion picture actors, directors, and studio executives seeking ranch-style homes close to studios in Studio City, Burbank, and Hollywood.
source_title: Valley Village History

fact: The Neighborhood Council Valley Village was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent the community bounded by Burbank Boulevard, the 170 Freeway, the 101 Freeway, and Coldwater Canyon.
source_title: Neighborhood Council Valley Village
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: In the 1960s and 1970s, Van Nuys Boulevard became famous across Southern California for its Wednesday night cruising culture, drawing thousands of customized cars and teenagers every week.
source_title: Cruising Van Nuys Boulevard: The Rise and Fall of a Valley Tradition

fact: Opened in 1928 as Metropolitan Airport in Van Nuys, Van Nuys Airport became one of the busiest general aviation airports in the world and served as a filming location for the final scene of Casablanca.
source_title: Van Nuys Airport History

fact: Completed in 1932 at 14410 Sylvan Street, the eight-story Art Deco Van Nuys City Hall (Marvin Braude San Fernando Valley Constituent Service Center) was the tallest building in the Valley for decades and is Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 202.
source_title: Van Nuys City Hall

fact: Founded in 1911 by Isaac Newton Van Nuys and his son-in-law James Benton Lankershim as 'The Town Started Right,' Van Nuys became the civic and governmental center of the San Fernando Valley.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: The Van Nuys Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent the civic core and surrounding residential neighborhoods of central Van Nuys.
source_title: Van Nuys Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Built in 1916 at 23533 West Justice Street in West Hills as a hunting lodge for Los Angeles Times general manager Harry Chandler, Shadow Ranch is designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 9.
source_title: Shadow Ranch Park
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: Situated along the western edge of West Hills in the Simi Hills, Upper Las Virgenes Canyon Open Space Preserve (Ahmanson Ranch) protects 2,983 acres of oak woodlands and coastal sage scrub.
source_title: Upper Las Virgenes Canyon Open Space Preserve

fact: The West Hills Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent the westernmost border of the City of Los Angeles adjacent to Ventura County.
source_title: West Hills Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Originally developed as the western portion of Canoga Park, the community was officially designated as the separate Los Angeles neighborhood of West Hills in 1987 following a resident petition.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: Shadow Ranch in West Hills was originally planted with thousands of eucalyptus trees by Albert Workman in the 1870s to supply timber and railroad ties across Southern California.
source_title: Shadow Ranch Park
source_publisher: City of Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks

fact: Charles Weeks named the settlement Winnetka after his former hometown of Winnetka, Illinois, which itself derived from a Potawatomi word meaning 'beautiful land.'
source_title: The Weeks Poultry Colony: Winnetka's Utopian Chicken-Farming Past

fact: Established in 1925 as Runnymede Elementary and renamed Winnetka Avenue Elementary School, the campus has served as a neighborhood anchor in Winnetka for over a century.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: The Winnetka Neighborhood Council was certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent residential and commercial neighborhoods between Canoga Park and Reseda.
source_title: Winnetka Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Winnetka was founded in 1922 by Charles Weeks as the 'Weeks Poultry Colony,' where settlers purchased one-acre plots to raise chickens and grow fruit trees under his intensive farming model.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: By 1928, the Weeks Poultry Colony in Winnetka had grown to more than 500 small farmsteads, making the community one of Southern California's leading egg-producing districts.
source_title: The Weeks Poultry Colony: Winnetka's Utopian Chicken-Farming Past

fact: Opened in 1947 on the 200-acre former estate of actor Jean Hersholt in Woodland Hills, the Motion Picture & Television Country House and Hospital provides retirement housing and healthcare for entertainment industry workers.
source_title: Motion Picture Country House

fact: In 1941, residents voted to rename the town of Girard to Woodland Hills in recognition of the dense tree canopy planted two decades earlier.
source_title: Victor Girard and the Creation of Woodland Hills

fact: Woodland Hills was founded in 1922 by developer Victor Girard as the master-planned community of Girard, where he planted more than 120,000 trees—including pepper, eucalyptus, and pine—to transform dry ranchland.
source_title: San Fernando Valley Communities: Name Origins and Brief History

fact: The Woodland Hills-Warner Center Neighborhood Council was officially certified by the Board of Neighborhood Commissioners in 2002 to represent both the hillside residential neighborhoods and the high-density Warner Center business district.
source_title: Woodland Hills-Warner Center Neighborhood Council
source_author: City of Los Angeles Department of Neighborhood Empowerment

fact: Warner Center was developed starting in the late 1960s on the former 1,100-acre Warner Ranch, once owned by motion picture pioneer Harry Warner of Warner Bros. Studios.
source_title: Warner Center 2035 Plan

fact: About 30,000 people gathered at the "Cascades" above the Valley on November 5, 1913 to watch Owens River water arrive through the LA Aqueduct.
source_title: Early Views of the San Fernando Valley

fact: Abbot Kinney opened "Venice of America" on July 4, 1905 to a crowd of 40,000.
source_title: About the Canals

fact: Venice's canals were dug with horses and mules starting in 1904, filled with tidal water from the Pacific.
source_title: Grand Design: The Canals of Venice (California)
source_author: Eleanor Boba
source_note: Photo: Herald-Examiner Collection, Los Angeles Public Library, Image #00057203.
